extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, literary critics, and educated readers interested in principles of epic poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical criteria for composing and evaluating epic (heroic) poetry—what subjects, styles, and fable-construction suit the genre, with examples from Milton, Homer, and Virgil. Emphasises probability vs. marvel, machinery, and suitable treatment of theological topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the nature and force of your genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace advises a Poet to consider thoroughly the Nature and Force of his Genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a subject that conforms to your particular talents (e.g., Milton chose a subject suited to his strength for the Sublime). Know where your power lies and select material that lets it operate fully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a subject conformable to your talents (noblest subject for the sublime)
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton's subject is 'the noblest that could have entered into the Thoughts of Man' because his genius was 'wonderfully turned to the Sublime.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your genius tends to the sublime, pick the grandest, most comprehensive subjects (creation, heaven, hell, the fall of man). A mismatch of subject and talent weakens the poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat divine or theological speech with restraint and devotional tone
rubrics_metrics.description: If Milton's Majesty forsakes him anywhere, it is in those Parts of his Poem, where the Divine Persons are introduced as Speakers; he confines himself to thoughts drawn from the Books of the most Orthodox Divines and to expressions found in Scripture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representing God or divine speech, prefer brevity, orthodoxy, and devotional clarity over purely poetical amplification; avoid giving the Almighty overly luxuriant imaginative language—aim to inspire devotion and religious awe rather than mere poetic grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use shortness and perspicuity when handling abstruse doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: The Particular Beauty of the Speeches in the Third Book consists in that Shortness and Perspicuity of Style, in which the Poet has couched the greatest Mysteries of Christianity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For difficult theological or philosophical material, be concise and clear; compress complex doctrines into a regular, lucid scheme so that general readers can grasp them and the poetry's grace can appear within those limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interperse poetic graces only where the subject admits them
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet is praised for the interspersing of all those Graces of Poetry, which the Subject was capable of receiving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't force ornamentation into parts of the poem ill-suited to it; embellish where the subject naturally permits, so graces enhance rather than distract from the matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance the probable and the marvellous in your fable (Aristotle's rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fable of an Epic Poem should abound in Circumstances that are both credible and astonishing; the Fable should be filled with the Probable and the Marvellous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a fable is only probable it reads like plain history; if only marvellous it becomes romance. The epic's secret is to produce both belief and astonishment simultaneously—use believable premises that admit wondrous outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconcile miracles by invoking agents of superior nature (machinery)
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet reconciles miracles with credibility by a happy Invention: introducing Agents of a superior Nature (gods, angels) who effect what is wonderful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you need extraordinary events, provide plausible supernatural agency or established mythic machinery so the marvel feels coherent within the poem's universe (examples: gods transforming ships, angels/spirits performing acts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid marvellous events that lack credible cause or intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples like Æneas tearing up the Myrtle that drops Blood (as presented from natural causes) are marvellous without probability; such incidents seem to have the Marvellous without the Probable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an extraordinary incident is represented as arising from natural causes without supernatural or believable justification, it strains credibility. Either supply a credible backstory (as Polydorus' tale explains the bleeding tree) or avoid such unexplained marvels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the plain literal sense of the fable appear probable to ordinary readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Besides hidden allegory, the plain literal Sense ought to appear Probable. The Story should be such as an ordinary Reader may acquiesce in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when the poem has allegorical depth, the surface narrative must be acceptable to common opinion and understanding; ground extraordinary elements in received beliefs or plausible detail so readers can suspend disbelief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic can admit the improbable/incredible more than tragedy (genre distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The surprising is necessary in tragedy; but the Epic Poem goes farther, and admits even the improbable and incredible, from which the highest degree of the surprising results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise genre conventions: epics have more latitude for the improbable (via machinery and scope) than tragedies, which rely more on credible human action—apply expectations accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historically known names or accepted authorities to increase credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancient tragic writers used the names of great men who had actually lived, tho the Tragedy proceeded upon Adventures they were never engaged in, on purpose to make the Subject more Credible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchoring fiction with familiar historical or legendary personages can lend plausibility to otherwise unlikely plots; the reader associates the characters with authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground imaginative choices in received opinions or philosophical doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton's choice (e.g., placing an angel in the Sun) is 'very finely contrived' and 'the more adjusted to a Poetical Probability' because it accords with 'a received Doctrine among the most famous Philosophers' that every orb had its intelligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When inventing grand images or cosmic arrangements, align them with prevailing philosophical, religious, or mythic beliefs to make them feel credible and resonant to contemporary readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: (Satirical) Personal breeding as a qualification for playwrights/poets
rubrics_metrics.description: Answer to 'what is the chief Qualification of a good Poet, especially of one who writes Plays'—To be a very well-bred Man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented humorously in the correspondence: social manners, taste, and understanding of genteel behaviour are implied as important for dramatists dealing with manners and society.
